1	# Architecture
2	
3	The §14 browser architecture as far as the §3 sea, the §6 encounters at sea and the §18 combat spike: browsers join a private match on one authoritative Colyseus room, the shared fixed-step simulation sails the ships over an authored tile map, and every browser draws what the server lets it see. A grapple that lands starts a 1v1 duel inside that room, fought with §15's prediction and rollback (the netcode is in `docs/duel.md`); the same duel also runs in a standalone duel room, for practice and private 1v1s.
4	
5	| Workspace | §14 component | What it holds now |
6	| --- | --- | --- |
7	| `apps/web` | Browser client and web shell | Landing page, HUD, keyboard helm (E and J latched), input sender, snapshot interpolation, one Phaser game per page: the sea scene (tile map, following camera, ships, telegraphs, duel markers, fogged minimap) and the arena scene; the duel client over a transport seam (keyboard with tap latch, `DuelClientSession` loop, duel HUD, dev-only latency setting) |
8	| `apps/server` | Match process | `MatchRoom` (one Colyseus room per match: the simulation, the encounter rules and its duels at sea), the Schema mirror, per-client views, input gate, entry points; `DuelRoom`; `DuelMachine`, the duel both rooms run, and its input gate; the shared private admission |
9	| `packages/simulation` | Shared fixed-step functions | Integer match state, heading table, sailing, collisions, docking, stopping and returning ships, visibility rule, seeded generator, `hashState`; the encounter rules (`/encounters`, `docs/encounters.md`); the duel (`/duel`) and its netcode (`/netcode`: `DuelAuthority`, `DuelRollback`, `DuelClock`, `DuelClientSession`, the input-delay policy) |
10	| `packages/protocol` | Data contracts (§16) | Protocol version (5), create and join options, the input schemas and validation (buttons: interact, grapple), the duel messages (with `duel-ready` at sea), refusal messages, the test-placement request |
11	| `packages/content` | Content and tuning (§17) | The slice sea (generated from Tiled), the Tiled converter, map validators, ship tuning, sight and engagement ranges, rules presets, frame budgets |
12	| `packages/test-tools` | Test harness (§17) | `HeadlessClient`: a browserless player on the real Colyseus SDK that also records the raw frames it receives, and fights at sea through its `fighter`; `HeadlessDuelClient` (the browser's `DuelClientSession` on the SDK, driven by a script, over a duel room or a match room), `ImpairmentProxy`, and `replayRecordedDuel` |
13	
14	The HTTP service, PostgreSQL, static hosting and monitoring are not built yet (`infra/` is a placeholder).
15	
16	## The sea
17	
18	- **Map format and pipeline.** The map is `assets/source/maps/slice-sea.tmj`, in a documented subset of Tiled's JSON format (`packages/content/src/tiledMap.ts`): orthogonal, finite, 24 px tiles (`TILE_PIXELS`, as drawn); one imageless tileset whose tiles carry a `type` of `sea`, `land`, `shoal` or `dock`; a `terrain` layer as a plain gid array; an `objects` layer with a named `island` rectangle per island (property `theme`), a `spawn` point per slot (properties `slot` and `facing`), one `hub` point and a `final-socket` rectangle per hidden final-island socket (properties `claimX`, `claimY`). Nothing else is accepted. `npm run map:build -- --from-sketch` writes it from one mirrored ASCII quarter (`sliceSeaSketch.ts`; a unit test fails when they differ). `npm run map:build` (`scripts/build-map.ts`) converts it into `packages/content/src/maps/sliceSea.ts` (terrain rows and objects) if it passes the validators; a unit test fails when that module is stale (it reads the `.tmj` as a Vite `?raw` import).
19	- **Validators.** `validateSeaMap` checks §2 and §3: four small islands, each land tile inside one island rectangle, each island with a dock beside its land and open sea; shoals; eight spawn slots on open sea outside the islands' bounding box and pairwise beyond `ENGAGEMENT_RANGE_TILES` (6); every dock and slot reachable by sea; and, by eight-way shortest paths (no cut corners) at full speed: each island's nearest neighbour 20–40 s away, no dock-or-slot crossing over 90 s, a dock within 40 s of every slot. No empty stretches: every navigable tile is within the sight radius of land, a shoal or a dock (not the edge). Routes meet: closing the disc around the hub (open sea near the centre; radius half the sight radius, so ships in it see each other) lengthens or cuts every shortest path between docks of different islands. At most 112 tiles a side. The slice sea (111 × 111 tiles, midline shoal walls open only in the hub's disc): neighbours 26 s apart, longest crossing 39 s, water within 9.9 tiles of an obstacle, 90 % open sea.
20	- **Final-island sockets (§3, §5).** `map.finalSockets` holds four identical dockless islets (one sketched islet, mirrored), each a rectangle of at most 6 × 6 and a claim tile: open sea beside it whose centre is the claim point, the treasure circle's centre (`TREASURE_CIRCLE_RADIUS_TILES`). Their land belongs to no island, so docks, sailing, respawn and visibility treat them as plain land. `validateFinalSockets` (run by `validateSeaMap`) requires every claim tile within 90 s of every spawn slot, at least two sockets in any sector holding one (`sectorOf`: column ⌊3x / width⌋, row ⌊3y / height⌋, the grid a sector reveal must use), at least 12 navigable tiles in each circle, and nothing within 8 tiles of what the running tests sail on (`keepClearZones`: the hub, spawn slots, docks and 14 tiles out from each, the out-of-sight row). The slice's sockets sit two in the north-centre sector and two in the south-centre one. `chooseFinalSocket(map, secret)` picks a match's socket from a 32-bit secret the server draws from a cryptographic source, mixed by the murmur3 finaliser before the modulo; never pass the public match seed (§3). Nothing uses the choice yet.
21	- **Sailing.** Positions are integer sub-units (256 a tile); headings are 64 directions, 0 east, clockwise (y grows down), unit vectors from a literal cosine table. Each world step the throttle (`-moveY`) accelerates towards 39 sub-units a step (3.05 tiles a second), brakes, or reverses slowly from a stop; `moveX` turns a heading a step (3.2 s a circle); none coasts to a stop. On 24 px tiles that handles like the old five tiles a second on 16 px (unit tests hold it within 25 %). The hull is a square of half-size 80. A move sweeps each axis in turn through the tile columns or rows its leading edge enters and stops flush at the first land, shoal or map edge: a ship slides along an obstacle met at an angle, runs aground head-on, and never tunnels.
22	- **Docking.** Hold E near a dock to moor, at any speed and throttle: with the hull on or beside the berth tile (unless pinched), or within reach with a clear run, it moves to the dock's centre, stops and records the dock, so no arrival slides past or grounds beside it (pinched: a diagonal tile whose two shared tiles are blocked). It stays moored while E or the throttle it moored with (`mooredThrottle`) is held; pressing a throttle after releasing that one, or the other direction, casts off. An input stall does not: the server gives a lapsed client no input, keeping the latch. The keyboard keeps a tap of E until its next read (not past a blur), the server until its next step; then the HUD says "Press E to dock".
23	- **Visibility boundary (§16).** The room's `ships` map is tagged `.view()`. Each client gets a `StateView`; after every mirror the room puts into it the client's own ship and each ship within `SIGHT_RADIUS_TILES` (10, `visibleShipIds`) and takes out the rest, so Colyseus encodes no other ship into that client's patches (an integration test checks the decoded state and the raw frames). `players` in the state is the public player count. Terrain is static content every client bundles, never synced; the minimap fog is client-side presentation, not a security boundary.
24	- **Test placement.** Tests place ships through `POST /__test/place` (code, session id, tile, heading); its tile bounds come from the map. Only the dev and test entry (`apps/server/src/dev.ts`) offers it, when `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_PLACEMENT=1`; the production entry (`main.ts`) never reads that, which the build smoke test checks. It only moves a ship: admission and views are unchanged.
25	
26	## Duels at sea (§6, §14)
27	
28	- **Encounters in the room.** Each world step (20 Hz), after sailing, `MatchRoom` builds one tick's snapshot for `stepEncounters` (`docs/encounters.md`): every ship's position and heading, whether its player is connected, pressed J since the last world step (the input gate latches it like E) and has a loaded arena. It passes back the reports of duels that ended since the last tick: the end, and with no rubbings yet the settlement on the same tick. It applies the events: `duel-reserved` stops both ships and opens a duel; `duel-started` starts its fight; a ready-check `duel-forfeited` or `duel-cancelled` ends it; `player-returned` and `player-respawned` move a ship (at rest, or moored at the dock). Everything else (attempts, protection, cooldowns, the loser's wait) is mirrored from the rules' state. The rules alone choose targets and decide hits, returns and docks; the room never re-implements them. Reserved and respawning ships get neutral input, so they stay put. Departure protection needs a match start, which private matches do not have yet, so no one starts protected.
29	- **One duel machine.** `DuelMachine` (`apps/server/src/duelMachine.ts`) is the duel both rooms run: seats and their `DuelInputGate`s, the 180-frame countdown with round-trip probes and the input delay chosen 30 frames before its end, `DuelAuthority` stepped at 60 Hz with a bundle every third frame, the reconnection bookkeeping (a dropped seat is marked away, a returning one gets a snapshot bundle) and the forfeits decided together at the next frame boundary. It writes a lobby schema and sends through a callback, so the host room owns clients and timers. `DuelRoom` starts the fight when the countdown ends (`start: "countdown"`); the match room starts it when the rules say so (`start: "called"`: the countdown is over and both fighters sent `duel-ready`). A countdown that ends with a fighter still loading waits in `waiting`, without probes; clients drop their session then, so the fight's clock starts from the fight's own frames. The match room keeps each duel's lobby for 2 s after settlement (`DUEL_RESULT_TICKS`), so both read the result.
30	- **Absence.** A fighter who drops keeps the seat for 10 s (`allowReconnection`, only during an unfinished duel) with the same view; the fight goes on with the input substituted as in any duel. Staying away or leaving forfeits (both on one frame: no winner, reported as cancelled). Outside a duel, leaving removes the ship as before.
31	- **Message routing.** A duel's `duel-frames` and `duel-probe` go to its two fighters only, with `client.send`; the room routes `duel-input`, `duel-probe` echoes and `duel-ready` from a session to that session's duel and drops them from anyone else. In the browser, `SeaDuelRouter` listens for the duel messages once per match and hands them to the duel client of the moment (a message that beats the lobby's patch waits for it); the same `DuelClient` runs a standalone duel over `duelRoomTransport`.
32	- **Visibility (§16).** The state's new maps are filtered per client like `ships`: `grapples` (telegraphs, keyed by attacker: in a view when its attacker is in sight, or when it is the viewer's own or aimed at the viewer), `markers` (a duel's position and reservation tick under an opaque key, nothing naming its fighters: in a view within the sight radius), `status` (a player's own mode, protection, cooldown and respawn tick: only the player's), `duels` (a duel's lobby: only its two fighters'). A ship in a duel or waiting to respawn is in no one else's view; its own player keeps it until it waits to respawn. A fighter or a player waiting to respawn sees no other ship, telegraph or marker. Integration tests check the decoded state and the raw frames of a watcher in sight and a stranger out of it.
33	- **One game per page.** The match page's Phaser game holds the sea scene and the arena scene (`MatchGame`); a duel puts the sea to sleep and starts the arena with that duel's client, and its end wakes the sea (`data-scene` says which shows). The duel HUD moves beside the canvas meanwhile. The standalone duel page's game holds only the arena. The helm is read during a duel (so a J tapped in the arena is not kept) but the sea gets neutral input.
34	
35	## The duel (combat spike)
36	
37	- **Duel room.** `DuelRoom` (room name `duel`) holds one duel, a `DuelMachine`: two players, or one in practice against a server-side dummy (player two, `idle` or `guard`). It is admitted like a match, by the same code in `admission.ts`: a one-time create token, `onAuth` before any seat, the room's own check, `filterBy(['code', 'createToken'])`, no token in the listing. The countdown (180 frames) starts once every seat is taken; the machine probes round trips during it, chooses the shared input delay 30 frames before the end, then steps `DuelAuthority` at 60 Hz, which the room's `setFixedTimestep` drives. Inputs go through `DuelInputGate`, which admits them through the same `InputAdmission` as the world's `InputGate` (the rate window and the protocol validation: 128 bytes, 60 a second of room ticks, increasing sequence, 30 frames of lead), so the two cannot drift, and counts its drops. Frame bundles and probes are Colyseus messages; the lobby is a small Schema state. A drop keeps the seat for 10 s (`allowReconnection`); leaving, or staying away, forfeits, decided at the next frame boundary (two forfeits on one frame: no winner). The rules and rates are in `docs/duel.md`.
38	- **One rollback core.** The browser's `DuelClient` and `HeadlessDuelClient` both run `DuelClientSession` from `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/netcode`; they differ only in transport and input (keyboard or script), and each plays over a duel room or a match room. The arena draws the predicted state; the HUD shows the confirmed one (server-equal health, stamina and clock) and the room's result. `window.__duel` exposes the session's counters and tagged inputs, read-only, for the browser tests.
39	- **Impairment harness.** `ImpairmentProxy` is a TCP proxy (Node's `net`, no new dependency) between a client and the server. It forwards HTTP untouched in content and splits the WebSocket stream into frames; each frame waits half the round trip plus a uniform ±jitter/2 in its direction, never overtaking the frame before it, and a lost frame (seeded draw) waits a further retransmission timeout (200 ms), stalling everything behind it as TCP does. `sever()` cuts every connection (optionally refusing new ones) for the reconnect tests. `tests/integration/duelHarness.test.ts` runs a scripted duel between two headless clients through it, with no impairment and at 80 ms, 20 ms jitter and 1 % loss (and `seaDuelHarness.test.ts` the same duel at sea, at 80 ms, 20 ms and 1 %, with the scripts and budget of `harness.ts`), and requires no desync at any of the ~180 hash checks per client, no rate-limited input, and corrections at most one per change of the opponent's applied input plus one per own substituted input, and at most 8 a second; it prints and annotates the counts. `replayRecordedDuel` replays a log (for example the pairs a client received) with `replayDuel`.
40	- **Dev latency.** Only in `npm run dev` (`import.meta.env.DEV`), `?rtt=80&jitter=20` on the page delays that browser's duel socket both ways, probes and pings included; the build smoke test checks the production bundle does not contain it. The browser checks run the production build, so the setting is tested below the browser: `apps/web/src/devLatency.ts` has no DOM dependency, unit tests with fake timers check its delay, jitter bound and order on a real SDK room, and `tests/integration/devLatency.test.ts` wraps two headless duel clients in it and checks that the room's measured round trip and chosen input delay rise above the same duel without it.
41	
42	## Rules the code keeps
43	
44	- **Purity.** `simulation`, `protocol` and `content` import no Phaser, Colyseus, DOM, timers, wall-clock time or `Math.random`, and call no floating-point transcendental `Math` function. Their tsconfig leaves out the DOM library, and `tests/unit/purity.test.ts` fails on a violation.
45	- **Integers.** Every number in the simulation state is an integer, so `hashState` (64-bit FNV-1a over a canonical serialization) does not depend on the JavaScript engine; a determinism test replays an input log.
46	- **One clock.** The room steps the simulation 60 times a second with Colyseus `setFixedTimestep`. World logic runs on frames divisible by 3 (20 Hz); the room then mirrors the plain state into its Schema and updates the views, and Colyseus patches clients at 20 Hz. Integration tests measure both rates, also with eight sailing ships in one cluster.
47	- **The server alone writes state.** At sea, clients send only `input` messages, `{seq, frame, buttons, moveX, moveY}`, validated with zod (the grapple is a button: the rules choose its target, never the client). `InputGate` drops, and counts, messages over the rate cap (60 per second of match time) or over 128 bytes, malformed ones (axes outside [-1, 1] are rejected, not clamped), ones whose sequence number is not higher than the last, and ones tagged more than 30 frames ahead. A held input lapses to neutral after 15 frames. An accepted world input applies from the server's next step whatever frame it names, since sea clients do not predict; a duel input applies to exactly the frame it names (`docs/duel.md`). Unknown message types are dropped. Colyseus's own limits sit above these: WebSocket frames over 4 KiB and more than 240 messages a second disconnect.
48	- **Joining.** Matches and duels share the admission code (`apps/server/src/admission.ts`). Colyseus serves `create`, `join`, `joinOrCreate` and `joinById` over HTTP and reserves a seat before any room check, so a private match is guarded in three layers. # Architecture

The §14 browser architecture as far as the §3 sea, the §6 encounters at sea and the §18 combat spike: browsers join a private match on one authoritative Colyseus room, the shared fixed-step simulation sails the ships over an authored tile map, and every browser draws what the server lets it see. A grapple that lands starts a 1v1 duel inside that room, fought with §15's prediction and rollback (the netcode is in `docs/duel.md`); the same duel also runs in a standalone duel room, for practice and private 1v1s.

| Workspace | §14 component | What it holds now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `apps/web` | Browser client and web shell | Landing page, HUD, keyboard helm (E and J latched), input sender, snapshot interpolation, one Phaser game per page: the sea scene (tile map, following camera, ships, telegraphs, duel markers, fogged minimap) and the arena scene; the duel client over a transport seam (keyboard with tap latch, `DuelClientSession` loop, duel HUD, dev-only latency setting) |
| `apps/server` | Match process | `MatchRoom` (one Colyseus room per match: the simulation, the encounter rules and its duels at sea), the Schema mirror, per-client views, input gate, entry points; `DuelRoom`; `DuelMachine`, the duel both rooms run, and its input gate; the shared private admission |
| `packages/simulation` | Shared fixed-step functions | Integer match state, heading table, sailing, collisions, docking, stopping and returning ships, visibility rule, seeded generator, `hashState`; the encounter rules (`/encounters`, `docs/encounters.md`); the duel (`/duel`) and its netcode (`/netcode`: `DuelAuthority`, `DuelRollback`, `DuelClock`, `DuelClientSession`, the input-delay policy) |
| `packages/protocol` | Data contracts (§16) | Protocol version (5), create and join options, the input schemas and validation (buttons: interact, grapple), the duel messages (with `duel-ready` at sea), refusal messages, the test-placement request |
| `packages/content` | Content and tuning (§17) | The slice sea (generated from Tiled), the Tiled converter, map validators, ship tuning, sight and engagement ranges, rules presets, frame budgets |
| `packages/test-tools` | Test harness (§17) | `HeadlessClient`: a browserless player on the real Colyseus SDK that also records the raw frames it receives, and fights at sea through its `fighter`; `HeadlessDuelClient` (the browser's `DuelClientSession` on the SDK, driven by a script, over a duel room or a match room), `ImpairmentProxy`, and `replayRecordedDuel` |

The HTTP service, PostgreSQL, static hosting and monitoring are not built yet (`infra/` is a placeholder).

## The sea

- **Map format and pipeline.** The map is `assets/source/maps/slice-sea.tmj`, in a documented subset of Tiled's JSON format (`packages/content/src/tiledMap.ts`): orthogonal, finite, 24 px tiles (`TILE_PIXELS`, as drawn); one imageless tileset whose tiles carry a `type` of `sea`, `land`, `shoal` or `dock`; a `terrain` layer as a plain gid array; an `objects` layer with a named `island` rectangle per island (property `theme`), a `spawn` point per slot (properties `slot` and `facing`), one `hub` point and a `final-socket` rectangle per hidden final-island socket (properties `claimX`, `claimY`). Nothing else is accepted. `npm run map:build -- --from-sketch` writes it from one mirrored ASCII quarter (`sliceSeaSketch.ts`; a unit test fails when they differ). `npm run map:build` (`scripts/build-map.ts`) converts it into `packages/content/src/maps/sliceSea.ts` (terrain rows and objects) if it passes the validators; a unit test fails when that module is stale (it reads the `.tmj` as a Vite `?raw` import).
- **Validators.** `validateSeaMap` checks §2 and §3: four small islands, each land tile inside one island rectangle, each island with a dock beside its land and open sea; shoals; eight spawn slots on open sea outside the islands' bounding box and pairwise beyond `ENGAGEMENT_RANGE_TILES` (6); every dock and slot reachable by sea; and, by eight-way shortest paths (no cut corners) at full speed: each island's nearest neighbour 20–40 s away, no dock-or-slot crossing over 90 s, a dock within 40 s of every slot. No empty stretches: every navigable tile is within the sight radius of land, a shoal or a dock (not the edge). Routes meet: closing the disc around the hub (open sea near the centre; radius half the sight radius, so ships in it see each other) lengthens or cuts every shortest path between docks of different islands. At most 112 tiles a side. The slice sea (111 × 111 tiles, midline shoal walls open only in the hub's disc): neighbours 26 s apart, longest crossing 39 s, water within 9.9 tiles of an obstacle, 90 % open sea.
- **Final-island sockets (§3, §5).** `map.finalSockets` holds four identical dockless islets (one sketched islet, mirrored), each a rectangle of at most 6 × 6 and a claim tile: open sea beside it whose centre is the claim point, the treasure circle's centre (`TREASURE_CIRCLE_RADIUS_TILES`). Their land belongs to no island, so docks, sailing, respawn and visibility treat them as plain land. `validateFinalSockets` (run by `validateSeaMap`) requires every claim tile within 90 s of every spawn slot, at least two sockets in any sector holding one (`sectorOf`: column ⌊3x / width⌋, row ⌊3y / height⌋, the grid a sector reveal must use), at least 12 navigable tiles in each circle, and nothing within 8 tiles of what the running tests sail on (`keepClearZones`: the hub, spawn slots, docks and 14 tiles out from each, the out-of-sight row). The slice's sockets sit two in the north-centre sector and two in the south-centre one. `chooseFinalSocket(map, secret)` picks a match's socket from a 32-bit secret the server draws from a cryptographic source, mixed by the murmur3 finaliser before the modulo; never pass the public match seed (§3). Nothing uses the choice yet.
- **Sailing.** Positions are integer sub-units (256 a tile); headings are 64 directions, 0 east, clockwise (y grows down), unit vectors from a literal cosine table. Each world step the throttle (`-moveY`) accelerates towards 39 sub-units a step (3.05 tiles a second), brakes, or reverses slowly from a stop; `moveX` turns a heading a step (3.2 s a circle); none coasts to a stop. On 24 px tiles that handles like the old five tiles a second on 16 px (unit tests hold it within 25 %). The hull is a square of half-size 80. A move sweeps each axis in turn through the tile columns or rows its leading edge enters and stops flush at the first land, shoal or map edge: a ship slides along an obstacle met at an angle, runs aground head-on, and never tunnels.
- **Docking.** Hold E near a dock to moor, at any speed and throttle: with the hull on or beside the berth tile (unless pinched), or within reach with a clear run, it moves to the dock's centre, stops and records the dock, so no arrival slides past or grounds beside it (pinched: a diagonal tile whose two shared tiles are blocked). It stays moored while E or the throttle it moored with (`mooredThrottle`) is held; pressing a throttle after releasing that one, or the other direction, casts off. An input stall does not: the server gives a lapsed client no input, keeping the latch. The keyboard keeps a tap of E until its next read (not past a blur), the server until its next step; then the HUD says "Press E to dock".
- **Visibility boundary (§16).** The room's `ships` map is tagged `.view()`. Each client gets a `StateView`; after every mirror the room puts into it the client's own ship and each ship within `SIGHT_RADIUS_TILES` (10, `visibleShipIds`) and takes out the rest, so Colyseus encodes no other ship into that client's patches (an integration test checks the decoded state and the raw frames). `players` in the state is the public player count. Terrain is static content every client bundles, never synced; the minimap fog is client-side presentation, not a security boundary.
- **Test placement.** Tests place ships through `POST /__test/place` (code, session id, tile, heading); its tile bounds come from the map. Only the dev and test entry (`apps/server/src/dev.ts`) offers it, when `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_PLACEMENT=1`; the production entry (`main.ts`) never reads that, which the build smoke test checks. It only moves a ship: admission and views are unchanged.

## Duels at sea (§6, §14)

- **Encounters in the room.** Each world step (20 Hz), after sailing, `MatchRoom` builds one tick's snapshot for `stepEncounters` (`docs/encounters.md`): every ship's position and heading, whether its player is connected, pressed J since the last world step (the input gate latches it like E) and has a loaded arena. It passes back the reports of duels that ended since the last tick: the end, and with no rubbings yet the settlement on the same tick. It applies the events: `duel-reserved` stops both ships and opens a duel; `duel-started` starts its fight; a ready-check `duel-forfeited` or `duel-cancelled` ends it; `player-returned` and `player-respawned` move a ship (at rest, or moored at the dock). Everything else (attempts, protection, cooldowns, the loser's wait) is mirrored from the rules' state. The rules alone choose targets and decide hits, returns and docks; the room never re-implements them. Reserved and respawning ships get neutral input, so they stay put. Departure protection needs a match start, which private matches do not have yet, so no one starts protected.
- **One duel machine.** `DuelMachine` (`apps/server/src/duelMachine.ts`) is the duel both rooms run: seats and their `DuelInputGate`s, the 180-frame countdown with round-trip probes and the input delay chosen 30 frames before its end, `DuelAuthority` stepped at 60 Hz with a bundle every third frame, the reconnection bookkeeping (a dropped seat is marked away, a returning one gets a snapshot bundle) and the forfeits decided together at the next frame boundary. It writes a lobby schema and sends through a callback, so the host room owns clients and timers. `DuelRoom` starts the fight when the countdown ends (`start: "countdown"`); the match room starts it when the rules say so (`start: "called"`: the countdown is over and both fighters sent `duel-ready`). A countdown that ends with a fighter still loading waits in `waiting`, without probes; clients drop their session then, so the fight's clock starts from the fight's own frames. The match room keeps each duel's lobby for 2 s after settlement (`DUEL_RESULT_TICKS`), so both read the result.
- **Absence.** A fighter who drops keeps the seat for 10 s (`allowReconnection`, only during an unfinished duel) with the same view; the fight goes on with the input substituted as in any duel. Staying away or leaving forfeits (both on one frame: no winner, reported as cancelled). Outside a duel, leaving removes the ship as before.
- **Message routing.** A duel's `duel-frames` and `duel-probe` go to its two fighters only, with `client.send`; the room routes `duel-input`, `duel-probe` echoes and `duel-ready` from a session to that session's duel and drops them from anyone else. In the browser, `SeaDuelRouter` listens for the duel messages once per match and hands them to the duel client of the moment (a message that beats the lobby's patch waits for it); the same `DuelClient` runs a standalone duel over `duelRoomTransport`.
- **Visibility (§16).** The state's new maps are filtered per client like `ships`: `grapples` (telegraphs, keyed by attacker: in a view when its attacker is in sight, or when it is the viewer's own or aimed at the viewer), `markers` (a duel's position and reservation tick under an opaque key, nothing naming its fighters: in a view within the sight radius), `status` (a player's own mode, protection, cooldown and respawn tick: only the player's), `duels` (a duel's lobby: only its two fighters'). A ship in a duel or waiting to respawn is in no one else's view; its own player keeps it until it waits to respawn. A fighter or a player waiting to respawn sees no other ship, telegraph or marker. Integration tests check the decoded state and the raw frames of a watcher in sight and a stranger out of it.
- **One game per page.** The match page's Phaser game holds the sea scene and the arena scene (`MatchGame`); a duel puts the sea to sleep and starts the arena with that duel's client, and its end wakes the sea (`data-scene` says which shows). The duel HUD moves beside the canvas meanwhile. The standalone duel page's game holds only the arena. The helm is read during a duel (so a J tapped in the arena is not kept) but the sea gets neutral input.

## The duel (combat spike)

- **Duel room.** `DuelRoom` (room name `duel`) holds one duel, a `DuelMachine`: two players, or one in practice against a server-side dummy (player two, `idle` or `guard`). It is admitted like a match, by the same code in `admission.ts`: a one-time create token, `onAuth` before any seat, the room's own check, `filterBy(['code', 'createToken'])`, no token in the listing. The countdown (180 frames) starts once every seat is taken; the machine probes round trips during it, chooses the shared input delay 30 frames before the end, then steps `DuelAuthority` at 60 Hz, which the room's `setFixedTimestep` drives. Inputs go through `DuelInputGate`, which admits them through the same `InputAdmission` as the world's `InputGate` (the rate window and the protocol validation: 128 bytes, 60 a second of room ticks, increasing sequence, 30 frames of lead), so the two cannot drift, and counts its drops. Frame bundles and probes are Colyseus messages; the lobby is a small Schema state. A drop keeps the seat for 10 s (`allowReconnection`); leaving, or staying away, forfeits, decided at the next frame boundary (two forfeits on one frame: no winner). The rules and rates are in `docs/duel.md`.
- **One rollback core.** The browser's `DuelClient` and `HeadlessDuelClient` both run `DuelClientSession` from `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/netcode`; they differ only in transport and input (keyboard or script), and each plays over a duel room or a match room. The arena draws the predicted state; the HUD shows the confirmed one (server-equal health, stamina and clock) and the room's result. `window.__duel` exposes the session's counters and tagged inputs, read-only, for the browser tests.
- **Impairment harness.** `ImpairmentProxy` is a TCP proxy (Node's `net`, no new dependency) between a client and the server. It forwards HTTP untouched in content and splits the WebSocket stream into frames; each frame waits half the round trip plus a uniform ±jitter/2 in its direction, never overtaking the frame before it, and a lost frame (seeded draw) waits a further retransmission timeout (200 ms), stalling everything behind it as TCP does. `sever()` cuts every connection (optionally refusing new ones) for the reconnect tests. `tests/integration/duelHarness.test.ts` runs a scripted duel between two headless clients through it, with no impairment and at 80 ms, 20 ms jitter and 1 % loss (and `seaDuelHarness.test.ts` the same duel at sea, at 80 ms, 20 ms and 1 %, with the scripts and budget of `harness.ts`), and requires no desync at any of the ~180 hash checks per client, no rate-limited input, and corrections at most one per change of the opponent's applied input plus one per own substituted input, and at most 8 a second; it prints and annotates the counts. `replayRecordedDuel` replays a log (for example the pairs a client received) with `replayDuel`.
- **Dev latency.** Only in `npm run dev` (`import.meta.env.DEV`), `?rtt=80&jitter=20` on the page delays that browser's duel socket both ways, probes and pings included; the build smoke test checks the production bundle does not contain it. The browser checks run the production build, so the setting is tested below the browser: `apps/web/src/devLatency.ts` has no DOM dependency, unit tests with fake timers check its delay, jitter bound and order on a real SDK room, and `tests/integration/devLatency.test.ts` wraps two headless duel clients in it and checks that the room's measured round trip and chosen input delay rise above the same duel without it.

## Rules the code keeps

- **Purity.** `simulation`, `protocol` and `content` import no Phaser, Colyseus, DOM, timers, wall-clock time or `Math.random`, and call no floating-point transcendental `Math` function. Their tsconfig leaves out the DOM library, and `tests/unit/purity.test.ts` fails on a violation.
- **Integers.** Every number in the simulation state is an integer, so `hashState` (64-bit FNV-1a over a canonical serialization) does not depend on the JavaScript engine; a determinism test replays an input log.
- **One clock.** The room steps the simulation 60 times a second with Colyseus `setFixedTimestep`. World logic runs on frames divisible by 3 (20 Hz); the room then mirrors the plain state into its Schema and updates the views, and Colyseus patches clients at 20 Hz. Integration tests measure both rates, also with eight sailing ships in one cluster.
- **The server alone writes state.** At sea, clients send only `input` messages, `{seq, frame, buttons, moveX, moveY}`, validated with zod (the grapple is a button: the rules choose its target, never the client). `InputGate` drops, and counts, messages over the rate cap (60 per second of match time) or over 128 bytes, malformed ones (axes outside [-1, 1] are rejected, not clamped), ones whose sequence number is not higher than the last, and ones tagged more than 30 frames ahead. A held input lapses to neutral after 15 frames. An accepted world input applies from the server's next step whatever frame it names, since sea clients do not predict; a duel input applies to exactly the frame it names (`docs/duel.md`). Unknown message types are dropped. Colyseus's own limits sit above these: WebSocket frames over 4 KiB and more than 240 messages a second disconnect.
- **Joining.** Matches and duels share the admission code (`apps/server/src/admission.ts`). Colyseus serves `create`, `join`, `joinOrCreate` and `joinById` over HTTP and reserves a seat before any room check, so a private match is guarded in three layers. The static `onAuth` runs before any seat is reserved: it refuses a mismatched protocol version (426), a request with neither or both of `code` and `createToken` or a malformed token (400), an unknown code (404) and a full match (409). A `create` carries a one-time 128-bit `createToken`; the room is registered with `filterBy(['code', 'createToken'])` and `onCreate` replaces the listing's metadata with `{code, custom}`, so no listing holds a token and a token-carrying request can only create. The room's `onJoin` is the backstop, and the only check `joinById` meets after `onAuth`: one seat with the creator's token, then only seats with the match's code (404 for another code, 403 otherwise). Refusal messages stay under 100 bytes. A caller who knows a room id can still hold seats with `joinById` until each reservation expires (15 s).
- **Rendering.** The client draws the ships the server sent 100 ms in the past, interpolating between patches; the HUD lists their latest decoded state. The camera follows the player's ship over a Phaser tile map at 24 px a tile (the 480 px sight circle fits the 800 × 560 view) that leaves open sea to the background colour, keeping a software renderer fast. The sea does not predict; the duel arena does (above), and uses Phaser's canvas renderer so a machine without a GPU keeps its main thread free for the 4 ms client tick.

## Toolchain

npm workspaces, TypeScript 7.0.2 (`tsc` for typechecks and package builds), Vite 8.3.0 (web build), Vitest 5.0.1 (`unit` and `integration` projects), tsx (map script and dev server), Phaser 4.2.1, `colyseus` 0.18.8 with `@colyseus/schema` 5.0.34, `@colyseus/sdk` 0.18.4, zod 4.6.5, Playwright 1.63.0. Workspace packages export a `@pirate-sea-race/source` condition that points at `src/`, so development and tests need no build. `npm run build` compiles each package to `dist/` in dependency order, then `scripts/smoke-build.ts` loads every workspace export from `dist/`, starts the built server on a free port, creates a match through the SDK, waits for the creator's ship and checks that no test-placement route answers, with every wait bounded. `colyseus` brings `uWebSockets.js` in from GitHub, so `npm ci` needs github.com as well as the npm registry. The duel added no dependency: `packages/test-tools` now also depends on the workspace's `@pirate-sea-race/simulation`, and the smoke test also loads `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/netcode` from `dist/`, checks the web bundle for the dev-only latency setting, and plays the first frames of a practice duel on the built server.

J: grapple the nearest ship ahead within six tiles; it lands after a second, unless the target sails out of range or out of its aim. A grapple that lands starts a duel.

    Status

    Round trip · input delay · corrections

    Move: WASD or the arrow keys (hold back to guard, down-back for lows). J light, K heavy, U and I specials, Shift dash, J and K together to throw (or to escape a throw). Down + K sweeps low, forward + K launches, down + J is the anti-air.

    import { Buttons } from "@pirate-sea-race/protocol"; /** What the player asks of their ship: protocol axes (moveX turns, moveY is the throttle, up ahead) and buttons. */ export interface Helm { readonly moveX: number; readonly moveY: number; readonly buttons: number; } export const NEUTRAL_HELM: Helm = { moveX: 0, moveY: 0, buttons: 0 }; const KEYS = { left: ["KeyA", "ArrowLeft"], right: ["KeyD", "ArrowRight"], up: ["KeyW", "ArrowUp"], down: ["KeyS", "ArrowDown"], interact: ["KeyE"], grapple: ["KeyJ"], } as const; /** Buttons kept from a tap until the next read: interact (E) and the grapple (J, §8). */ const LATCHED: readonly [readonly string[], number][] = [ [KEYS.interact, Buttons.Interact], [KEYS.grapple, Buttons.Grapple], ]; const HELM_CODES = new Set(Object.values(KEYS).flat()); /** Converts two opposing keys into one axis: both held is neutral, whatever order they were pressed in (§8). */ export function axis(negative: boolean, positive: boolean): number { return (positive ? 1 : 0) - (negative ? 1 : 0); } /** * The keyboard input adapter (§8 defaults): up is throttle, down brakes (and reverses slowly from a stop), left and * right turn, E interacts (docks), J grapples. It tracks held keys and releases them all (and forgets a tap) when the * window loses focus, so a ship never keeps sailing, docks or grapples on a key the page missed. The page reads it on * a timer, so a tap of E or J that goes down and up between two reads is kept until the next read, as the duel * keyboard keeps its taps: it counts once. */ export class KeyboardHelm { private readonly held = new Set(); private tapped = 0; constructor(target: Window) { target.addEventListener("keydown", (event) => { if (!HELM_CODES.has(event.code) || isTyping(event.target)) return; event.preventDefault(); this.press(event.code); }); target.addEventListener("keyup", (event) => this.release(event.code)); target.addEventListener("blur", () => { this.held.clear(); this.tapped = 0; }); } press(code: string): void { if (!HELM_CODES.has(code)) return; this.held.add(code); for (const [codes, button] of LATCHED) if (codes.includes(code)) this.tapped |= button; } release(code: string): void { this.held.delete(code); } /** What is held now, plus a button tapped since the last read. Reading it clears the tap. */ helm(): Helm { const any = (codes: readonly string[]) => codes.some((code) => this.held.has(code)); let buttons = this.tapped; for (const [codes, button] of LATCHED) if (any(codes)) buttons |= button; this.tapped = 0; return { moveX: axis(any(KEYS.left), any(KEYS.right)), moveY: axis(any(KEYS.up), any(KEYS.down)), buttons, }; } } /** Whether a key went to a text field. Outside a browser (unit tests in Node) there are no text fields. */ function isTyping(target: EventTarget | null): boolean { return ( (typeof HTMLInputElement !== "undefined" && target instanceof HTMLInputElement) || (typeof HTMLTextAreaElement !== "undefined" && target instanceof HTMLTextAreaElement) ); } import { MAX_INPUT_LEAD_FRAMES, MessageType, type InputMessage } from "@pirate-sea-race/protocol"; import { STEPS_PER_SECOND } from "@pirate-sea-race/simulation"; import { NEUTRAL_HELM, type Helm } from "./keyboard.js"; /** Resend a held input this often, well inside the server's 250 ms hold window. */ const REFRESH_MS = 100; /** Never tag an input further ahead than half the server's future-frame window. */ const MAX_ESTIMATE_LEAD = Math.floor(MAX_INPUT_LEAD_FRAMES / 2); /** The client's estimate of the server's current frame: the last patched frame plus the time since it arrived. */ export function estimateServerFrame(patchedFrame: number, patchedAt: number, now: number): number { const elapsed = Math.max(0, Math.floor(((now - patchedAt) * STEPS_PER_SECOND) / 1000)); return patchedFrame + Math.min(elapsed, MAX_ESTIMATE_LEAD); } export interface InputChannel { send(type: string, message: InputMessage): void; } /** Sends the player's intent: on every change, and repeated while a key is held. */ export class InputSender { private seq = 0; private last: Helm = NEUTRAL_HELM; private lastSentAt = Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY; private patchedFrame = 0; private patchedAt = 0; constructor(private readonly channel: InputChannel) {} observeFrame(frame: number, now: number): void { if (frame !== this.patchedFrame) { this.patchedFrame = frame; this.patchedAt = now; } } update(helm: Helm, now: number): void { const changed = helm.moveX !== this.last.moveX || helm.moveY !== this.last.moveY || helm.buttons !== this.last.buttons; const held = helm.moveX !== 0 || helm.moveY !== 0 || helm.buttons !== 0; if (!changed && !(held && now - this.lastSentAt >= REFRESH_MS)) return; this.channel.send(MessageType.Input, { seq: ++this.seq, frame: estimateServerFrame(this.patchedFrame, this.patchedAt, now), buttons: helm.buttons, moveX: helm.moveX, moveY: helm.moveY, }); this.last = helm; this.lastSentAt = now; } }

lines: /** The client and server must speak the same protocol version to join (§17). Bump it on any message change. */
/** The Colyseus room name of a match. */
+ * The rubbing messages (protocol v6, §4 and §16). Collecting at a source and claiming from a recovery cache need no
+ * message of their own: the player holds interact (E) moored at the dock, and the server decides the target. The one
+ * new client message is the theft choice.
+  /** Client → server: the winner of a duel picks the rubbing type to steal (`ChooseTheftMessage`). */
+ * The four rubbing types in the fixed type order (content's `RUBBING_TYPES`, which the protocol does not depend on).
+ * A server unit test keeps the two equal.
+/** The largest theft choice accepted, measured as its JSON encoding. A valid one is under 40 bytes. */
+/** Theft choices a client may send per second before the server drops the rest. */
+ * §16: a theft choice refers to a server-created duel result (`duel`, the opaque key of the winner's own duel lobby)
+ * and names one type. It is not a transfer request: the server checks that the sender won that duel, that its choice
+ * window is open and that the type is eligible, and otherwise changes nothing.
+/** Validates an untrusted theft choice: its size, then its schema. */
+  if (size === undefined || size > MAX_CHOOSE_THEFT_BYTES) return undefined;
+ * Test-only source layout (§4 assignment, pinned for tests). The server deals the rubbings onto the island sources
+ * with its own private randomness; a scenario that needs "a Sun island" and "a Moon island" cannot know which is
+ * which. With this setting the dev and test entry (never the production `main`) deals them in a fixed layout instead:
+ * one island per `|`-separated group, in island order, each group the types of that island's sources in source order,
+ * for example `sun,sun|moon,moon|sun,sun|moon,moon`. It is off unless the variable is set, and the layout must still
+ * pass the ledger's assignment validation (every rubbing sealed once).
+/** Parses a test source layout: island groups of rubbing type names, or undefined when it is malformed. */

content.content:
# Pirate Sea Race

A browser multiplayer pirate treasure race. The game is specified in [`docs/spec.md`](docs/spec.md) (the text of `docs/spec.docx`); [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) maps this repository onto it.

Browsers create or join a private match by a six-character code and sail placeholder ships around the slice sea: a compact map with four small islands with docks, reefs and shoal walls that funnel every route between islands through one central crossing, and eight outer-sea spawn slots. Up (or W) sails ahead, down (S) brakes and then reverses, left and right (A, D) turn, and E docks a ship beside a dock, at any speed. The authoritative server decides every position and sends each browser only the ships within its sight radius; the minimap's fog clears where the player has sailed.

Fights happen at sea (§6): J grapples the nearest ship ahead within six tiles. The attacker sees its aim, the target a warning with the side it comes from, and it lands after a one-second windup unless the target sails out of range or out of the aim (a miss costs six seconds). A grapple that lands stops both ships; after a three-second countdown the two fight the online duel inside the match, in the same page's arena, while everyone else in sight sees crossed swords and the elapsed time where they fight. The winner sails on with eight seconds of protection; the loser respawns at a dock 15 seconds after the fight, with 20 seconds of protection; a draw returns both to separate nearby points. A fighter who drops has ten seconds to come back to the same fight; leaving forfeits.

The standalone duel (the combat spike, §18 stage 1) runs beside it: "Create duel" makes a 1v1 duel whose code the second browser enters under "Join duel", and "Practice" fights a server-side dummy (idle or guarding). After a three-second countdown both browsers predict the fight with the shared duel simulation and roll back to the server's inputs (`docs/duel.md`). Keys (§8): WASD or the arrows move (hold back to guard), J light, K heavy, U and I specials, Shift dash, J and K together throw. The HUD shows both health bars, stamina, the round clock, the connection line (round trip, input delay, corrections) and the result; "Show hitboxes" draws hurtboxes and active hitboxes.

## Requirements

Node 24 and npm 11. The browser tests use Playwright's Chromium for `@playwright/test` 1.63.0, which must already be installed.

## Commands

Run these from the repository root.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Install | `npm ci` |
| Develop (server on 2593, web on 5393, both from source) | `npm run dev` |
| Typecheck every workspace | `npm run typecheck` |
| Unit tests | `npm run test:unit` |
| Integration tests (a real server in-process, headless clients) | `npm run test:integration` |
| Build every package and the web client, then smoke-test the built server | `npm run build` |
| Convert the Tiled map `assets/source/maps/slice-sea.tmj` into `packages/content/src/maps/sliceSea.ts` (validated first) | `npm run map:build` |
| Check that the generated map module is up to date (a unit test checks this too) | `npm run map:check` |
| Run the built server | `npm start` |
| Browser tests (start the server and web client themselves) | `npx --no-install playwright test --config=tests/e2e/playwright.config.ts` |

Set `VITE_SERVER_URL` when the web client should reach a server other than port 2593 on its own host.

**Simulated latency for duel playtests (development only).** With `npm run dev`, add `?rtt=80&jitter=20` to the page's address (for example `http://localhost:5393/?rtt=80&jitter=20`) before creating or joining a duel: that browser's duel socket is then delayed by half the round trip each way, plus a uniform ±jitter/2, in order, round-trip probes included, so the HUD's round trip and the chosen input delay reflect it. Give both browsers the setting to test §19's 30, 80 or 150 ms. It is read only when `import.meta.env.DEV` is true and is absent from the production build (`npm run build` checks). Loss is simulated only by the test harness (`ImpairmentProxy` in `packages/test-tools`).

The map is generated from an ASCII sketch of one quarter, `assets/source/maps/sliceSeaSketch.ts`: edit it, then run `npm run map:build -- --from-sketch` (details in `assets/source/maps/README.md`). The `.tmj` stays within the Tiled subset documented in `packages/content/src/tiledMap.ts`, so [Tiled](https://www.mapeditor.org/) opens it.

`PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_PLACEMENT=1` is a test-only setting, off by default: the dev and test entry point (`npm run dev`, and the server the browser tests start) then serves `POST /__test/place`, which puts a player's ship on a chosen tile. The production entry (`npm start`) never reads it.

## Layout

| Path | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `apps/web` | Phaser client: landing page, HUD, input, interpolated rendering, the duel arena and HUD |
| `apps/server` | Colyseus match and duel server |
| `packages/simulation` | Pure fixed-step simulation shared by client and server, the duel and its rollback netcode |
| `packages/protocol` | Message schemas, validation and the protocol version |
| `packages/content` | The generated sea map, the Tiled converter, map validators, tuning, rules presets and frame budgets |
| `packages/test-tools` | Headless match and duel clients, the network impairment proxy and the duel replay wrapper |
| `tests/unit`, `tests/integration`, `tests/e2e` | Cross-package unit tests, server integration tests, Playwright scenarios |
| `assets/source/maps` | The Tiled source map and the sketch it is generated from |
| `assets/source`, `assets/exported`, `infra` | Placeholders for art sources, runtime assets and deployment |
3:The pure 1v1 duel of §7 and §8 with the Duelist kit. `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/duel` has the step, snapshots and replay. `@pirate-sea-race/content/moves` has the move data, rules, validators and the input log schema. The code has no clocks, no `Math.random` and uses integer maths only.
64:- Log JSON: `{ "format": "pirate-sea-race/duel-input-log", "version": 1, "movesetVersion": "a32af270c3979db5", "startFrame": N, "inputs": [[p1, p2], …] }`, where `inputs[i]` is frame N + i + 1. `duelInputLogSchema` validates it. A replay is refused for a malformed log, another moveset version, or a `startFrame` that is not the state's frame.
70:§15's server-authoritative prediction and rollback, in `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/netcode` (pure: the caller passes the time). `DuelAuthority` is the server's half, `DuelClientSession` (the clock, the input stream and `DuelRollback`) the client's; the browser and the headless test client run the same session. On the server, `DuelMachine` (`apps/server`) runs one duel around `DuelAuthority`, the same in a standalone `DuelRoom` and inside a `MatchRoom` (below).
83:| client → server | `duel-ready` | `{}`: this fighter's arena is loaded (duels at sea) | once per duel |
85:Each frame travels in two input messages, so one lost message costs nothing. The world input gate's limits apply unchanged: 128 bytes, 60 messages a second, increasing `seq`, `frame` at most 30 frames past the server's. The lobby (code, phase, countdown, seed, input delay, seats, result) is the room's Schema state.
103:**Reconnect** (§12). A player who drops keeps their seat for 10 seconds (Colyseus `allowReconnection`); meanwhile the server substitutes their input as above, so they fall to neutral after 250 ms. The SDK reconnects on its own; the room sends the returning client a snapshot bundle, from which it continues. Absent past 10 seconds, or quitting once the countdown has begun, forfeits. Forfeits are decided together at the next frame boundary, so the order the room processes two leaves in never picks a winner (§7): one forfeit is the opponent's win by `forfeit`, even when the opponent is away but still inside their own window; both on the same frame is a result with no winner (`winner` −1, reason `forfeit`, "Both forfeit: no winner"), so nothing is awarded.
107:## Inside a match room (`encounters-online`)
109:§14: a duel at sea is a simulation object of the match room, not a room of its own. A grapple that lands (`duel-reserved` from the encounter rules, `docs/encounters.md`) opens one: a `DuelMachine` with the attacker as player one and the grappled player as player two, a fresh seed, and its lobby in the match state's `duels` map under an opaque key. Its countdown starts at once. Fighters, their frames and their result are exactly a duel room's: the same machine, messages, gates, rates, input delay, bundles, hash checks and forfeits. What differs:
111:- **Start.** The machine's fight starts when the room calls `start()`, on the rules' `duel-started`: the 3 s countdown is over and both fighters have sent `duel-ready` (the browser sends it once its arena scene is up, the headless client when the lobby appears). A countdown that ends first leaves the lobby in `waiting`, with no probes, and clients drop their session: the fight's clock then starts from its own frame-0 snapshot rather than from a countdown that stopped. A fighter still not ready 10 s after the grapple forfeits, both cancels (reason `cancelled`, winner −1): the rules decide it and the room ends the machine.
112:- **End.** The machine's result (a KO, the clock, a forfeit) goes back to the rules at the next world tick as an end report (a win, a draw, or `cancelled` for a double forfeit), and, with no rubbings to steal yet, the settlement on the same tick. The winner goes back to its own position with 8 s of protection; the loser waits 15 s from that end tick and respawns at the dock the rules choose with 20 s; a draw returns both to separate points. The lobby stays in the fighters' views for 2 s more with the result, then the clients return to the sea.
113:- **Absence.** A fighter who drops during an unfinished duel keeps the seat for 10 s (`allowReconnection`, the same view); the SDK reconnects on its own and the machine sends a snapshot bundle to continue from. Past 10 s, or on leaving the match, the fighter forfeits (and the ship leaves the match).
115:- **Clients.** The browser's `DuelClient` takes a `DuelTransport`: `duelRoomTransport(room)` for a duel room, `SeaDuelRouter.transport(key)` inside a match (the router listens for duel messages once per match and holds any that beat the lobby). `HeadlessDuelClient` does the same (`HeadlessClient.fighter`). Kits come later (`fruit-kits-online`): a duel at sea is the Duelist mirror.

A fighter who drops has ten seconds to come back to the same fight; leaving forfeits.

The standalone duel (the combat spike, §18 stage 1) runs beside it: "Create duel" makes a 1v1 duel whose code the second browser enters under "Join duel", and "Practice" fights a server-side dummy (idle or guarding). After a three-second countdown both browsers predict the fight with the shared duel simulation and roll back to the server's inputs (`docs/duel.md`). Keys (§8): WASD or the arrows move (hold back to guard), J light, K heavy, U and I specials, Shift dash, J and K together throw. The HUD shows both health bars, stamina, the round clock, the connection line (round trip, input delay, corrections) and the result; "Show hitboxes" draws hurtboxes and active hitboxes.

## Requirements

Node 24 and npm 11. The browser tests use Playwright's Chromium for `@playwright/test` 1.63.0, which must already be installed.

## Commands

Run these from the repository root.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Install | `npm ci` |
| Develop (server on 2593, web on 5393, both from source) | `npm run dev` |
| Typecheck every workspace | `npm run typecheck` |
| Unit tests | `npm run test:unit` |
| Integration tests (a real server in-process, headless clients) | `npm run test:integration` |
| Build every package and the web client, then smoke-test the built server | `npm run build` |
| Convert the Tiled map `assets/source/maps/slice-sea.tmj` into `packages/content/src/maps/sliceSea.ts` (validated first) | `npm run map:build` |
| Check that the generated map module is up to date (a unit test checks this too) | `npm run map:check` |
| Run the built server | `npm start` |
| Browser tests (start the server and web client themselves) | `npx --no-install playwright test --config=tests/e2e/playwright.config.ts` |

Set `VITE_SERVER_URL` when the web client should reach a server other than port 2593 on its own host.

**Simulated latency for duel playtests (development only).** With `npm run dev`, add `?rtt=80&jitter=20` to the page's address (for example `http://localhost:5393/?rtt=80&jitter=20`) before creating or joining a duel: that browser's duel socket is then delayed by half the round trip each way, plus a uniform ±jitter/2, in order, round-trip probes included, so the HUD's round trip and the chosen input delay reflect it. Give both browsers the setting to test §19's 30, 80 or 150 ms. It is read only when `import.meta.env.DEV` is true and is absent from the production build (`npm run build` checks). Loss is simulated only by the test harness (`ImpairmentProxy` in `packages/test-tools`).

The map is generated from an ASCII sketch of one quarter, `assets/source/maps/sliceSeaSketch.ts`: edit it, then run `npm run map:build -- --from-sketch` (details in `assets/source/maps/README.md`). The `.tmj` stays within the Tiled subset documented in `packages/content/src/tiledMap.ts`, so [Tiled](https://www.mapeditor.org/) opens it.

`PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_PLACEMENT=1` is a test-only setting, off by default: the dev and test entry point (`npm run dev`, and the server the browser tests start) then serves `POST /__test/place`, which puts a player's ship on a chosen tile. The production entry (`npm start`) never reads it.

3:The pure 1v1 duel of §7 and §8 with the Duelist kit. `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/duel` has the step, snapshots and replay. `@pirate-sea-race/content/moves` has the move data, rules, validators and the input log schema. The code has no clocks, no `Math.random` and uses integer maths only.
64:- Log JSON: `{ "format": "pirate-sea-race/duel-input-log", "version": 1, "movesetVersion": "a32af270c3979db5", "startFrame": N, "inputs": [[p1, p2], …] }`, where `inputs[i]` is frame N + i + 1. `duelInputLogSchema` validates it. A replay is refused for a malformed log, another moveset version, or a `startFrame` that is not the state's frame.
70:§15's server-authoritative prediction and rollback, in `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/netcode` (pure: the caller passes the time). `DuelAuthority` is the server's half, `DuelClientSession` (the clock, the input stream and `DuelRollback`) the client's; the browser and the headless test client run the same session. On the server, `DuelMachine` (`apps/server`) runs one duel around `DuelAuthority`, the same in a standalone `DuelRoom` and inside a `MatchRoom` (below).
83:| client → server | `duel-ready` | `{}`: this fighter's arena is loaded (duels at sea) | once per duel |
85:Each frame travels in two input messages, so one lost message costs nothing. The world input gate's limits apply unchanged: 128 bytes, 60 messages a second, increasing `seq`, `frame` at most 30 frames past the server's. The lobby (code, phase, countdown, seed, input delay, seats, result) is the room's Schema state.
103:**Reconnect** (§12). A player who drops keeps their seat for 10 seconds (Colyseus `allowReconnection`); meanwhile the server substitutes their input as above, so they fall to neutral after 250 ms. The SDK reconnects on its own; the room sends the returning client a snapshot bundle, from which it continues. Absent past 10 seconds, or quitting once the countdown has begun, forfeits. Forfeits are decided together at the next frame boundary, so the order the room processes two leaves in never picks a winner (§7): one forfeit is the opponent's win by `forfeit`, even when the opponent is away but still inside their own window; both on the same frame is a result with no winner (`winner` −1, reason `forfeit`, "Both forfeit: no winner"), so nothing is awarded.
107:## Inside a match room (`encounters-online`)
109:§14: a duel at sea is a simulation object of the match room, not a room of its own. A grapple that lands (`duel-reserved` from the encounter rules, `docs/encounters.md`) opens one: a `DuelMachine` with the attacker as player one and the grappled player as player two, a fresh seed, and its lobby in the match state's `duels` map under an opaque key. Its countdown starts at once. Fighters, their frames and their result are exactly a duel room's: the same machine, messages, gates, rates, input delay, bundles, hash checks and forfeits. What differs:
111:- **Start.** The machine's fight starts when the room calls `start()`, on the rules' `duel-started`: the 3 s countdown is over and both fighters have sent `duel-ready` (the browser sends it once its arena scene is up, the headless client when the lobby appears). A countdown that ends first leaves the lobby in `waiting`, with no probes, and clients drop their session: the fight's clock then starts from its own frame-0 snapshot rather than from a countdown that stopped. A fighter still not ready 10 s after the grapple forfeits, both cancels (reason `cancelled`, winner −1): the rules decide it and the room ends the machine.
112:- **End.** The machine's result (a KO, the clock, a forfeit) goes back to the rules at the next world tick as an end report (a win, a draw, or `cancelled` for a double forfeit), and, with no rubbings to steal yet, the settlement on the same tick. The winner goes back to its own position with 8 s of protection; the loser waits 15 s from that end tick and respawns at the dock the rules choose with 20 s; a draw returns both to separate points. The lobby stays in the fighters' views for 2 s more with the result, then the clients return to the sea.
113:- **Absence.** A fighter who drops during an unfinished duel keeps the seat for 10 s (`allowReconnection`, the same view); the SDK reconnects on its own and the machine sends a snapshot bundle to continue from. Past 10 s, or on leaving the match, the fighter forfeits (and the ship leaves the match).
115:- **Clients.** The browser's `DuelClient` takes a `DuelTransport`: `duelRoomTransport(room)` for a duel room, `SeaDuelRouter.transport(key)` inside a match (the router listens for duel messages once per match and holds any that beat the lobby). `HeadlessDuelClient` does the same (`HeadlessClient.fighter`). | The ledger settles the duel (a draw or cancellation at once, a win at `chooseTheft` or `advanceLedger`) | A `settled` report with the ledger's settlement tick. |
| `player-returned`, `player-respawned` | Move the ship (or player) to `x, y`. `protection` is also the claim's `protected` flag. |
-| `stepClaim` emits `protection-ended`, or the ledger starts a collection | Set `protectionEndedBy` next tick. |
+| `stepClaim` emits `protection-ended`, or the ledger starts a collection or a cache claim | Set `protectionEndedBy` next tick (`collection` for both ledger holds). |
| `stepClaim` emits `match-ended` (its `duel-ended-without-theft` ends running duels) | Set `matchOver: true` next tick. |

-`MatchRoom` runs the step each world tick, after sailing: every ship is a `ship` player, `attack` is the grapple button (J) latched since the last world step, `ready` is the fighter's `duel-ready`, and `connected` whether its client is there (a fighter who dropped is away until it reconnects or its 10 s run out). There is no claim channel or ledger yet: `protectionEndedBy` is always null and `matchOver` false. A fight that ends is reported at the next tick as an `end` and, with no theft yet, a `settled` on the same tick; a `duel-forfeited` or `duel-cancelled` from the ready check gets only the `settled`. Nobody starts with spawn protection, because a private match has no start of play yet. The room's own part (the duel machine, the returns, what each client may see) is in `docs/architecture.md` and `docs/duel.md`.

+`MatchRoom` runs the step each world tick, after sailing: every ship is a `ship` player, `attack` is the grapple button (J) latched since the last world step, `ready` is the fighter's `duel-ready`, and `connected` whether its client is there (a disconnected ship stays in the snapshot for its seat's 60 s, so it can be grappled, §12). `matchOver` is false until `objectives-endgame`.
+Since `rubbings-theft` the room maps the rules onto the objective ledger as the table above says. Per world tick, in this order:
+1. `advanceLedger`: choice windows that closed settle with the default theft.

+2. The §12 timers, on the same tick: a fighter away from an unfinished duel for 10 s is forfeited in its machine; a disconnected player whose seat deadline has come is expired in the ledger (their rubbings into a cache at the dock `respawnPoint` would choose for them) and their ship leaves.

+3. `stepEncounters`, with the reports: a fight that ended since the last tick is reported to the ledger (`reportDuelResult`, unless a player's quit or expiry already decided it there) and its `end` goes to the rules as the ledger recorded it; a `settled` report goes for each duel the ledger has settled, never before. A duel's players therefore return only after the settlement. `duel-reserved` calls `reserveDuel`; a ready-check `duel-forfeited` or `duel-cancelled` calls `reportDuelResult` and gets no `end` report back.

+4. The ledger's holds: each connected player moored at a dock and holding E continues, starts or (without E, mooring or a target) cancels a collection or a cache claim. A hold that starts sets `protectionEndedBy: "collection"` for the next tick, so collecting or claiming ends protection (§2, §6) one tick (50 ms) late.

+A theft choice (`choose-theft`) arrives between ticks and calls `chooseTheft` at the last processed tick; its settlement is reported on the next tick. Nobody starts with spawn protection, because a private match has no start of play yet. The room's own part (the duel machine, the returns, what each client may see) is in `docs/architecture.md` and `docs/duel.md`.
- Island walking doesn't exist yet. The island challenge is tested for timing, range, cone and cooldown only, with caller-supplied positions.

-The pure rubbing ledger of §4 with duel settlement (§11's theft and PvP gold), §12's recovery caches and §11's small match economy. `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/objectives` has the state, the operations and the invariant. `@pirate-sea-race/content/objectives` has the types, rubbing ids, timings, the gold and economy rules and the zod validators for source sites and assignments. It is plain integer data with no clocks and no `Math.random`. Time is the world tick (20 per second), supplied by the caller. Positions are integer sub-units, supplied by the caller. Nothing here is wired into `MatchRoom` yet.

+The pure rubbing ledger of §4 with duel settlement (§11's theft and PvP gold), §12's recovery caches and §11's small match economy. `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/objectives` has the state, the operations and the invariant. `@pirate-sea-race/content/objectives` has the types, rubbing ids, timings, the gold and economy rules and the zod validators for source sites and assignments. It is plain integer data with no clocks and no `Math.random`. Time is the world tick (20 per second), supplied by the caller. Positions are integer sub-units, supplied by the caller. `MatchRoom` runs it since `rubbings-theft` (below, and `docs/architecture.md`).
- **The invariant** becomes balances + `goldSpent` = `goldIssued`, with `goldIssued` = purses + grants.

- **Rumor flow:** the room first asks the intel module whether a targeted rumor is available for the player (a missing type with a lead). Only then does it call `purchase` with the client's request id. On `ok && !replayed` it asks intel to deliver the rumor under that (player, request id). On `ok && replayed` it resends the rumor already delivered. On `!ok` (`replayed` or not) it sends the refusal and delivers nothing: a `replayed` refusal is the original answer, so a delayed retry never buys what the player was refused. A rumor that cannot be delivered is never bought.

+- **One ledger per match**, the `slice` preset, seeded from the room's own private randomness (never the public match code). Its sites are each regular island's docks, `sourcesPerIsland` (2) per island in dock id order, reusing a dock when an island has fewer (`apps/server/src/objectives.ts`). **Until the ruins are wired (`objectives-endgame`), every source is unlocked at match start**; the ruins feature will lock them behind its puzzles.

+- **Holding E** moored at a dock of island *i* works on its first eligible target: the island's sealed, unlocked source of a type the player lacks, else a rubbing of a type they lack in a recovery cache at that dock, each in the fixed type order. The room calls `startCollect`/`startCacheClaim`, then `progressChannel` every held tick, and `cancelChannel` when E is released, the ship casts off or the target is gone. A reservation (`reserveDuel`) and a disconnect cancel it inside the ledger.
+- **Duels** follow `docs/encounters.md`'s mapping; the room reports `settled` to the rules only once the ledger has settled.

+- **§12** runs on the world tick: `disconnectPlayer` at a drop, `reconnectPlayer` on return, `expireReservation` at the deadline (the cache at the dock the rules would respawn the player at), `quitPlayer` for every other leave (the cache at the dock nearest the ship by sea).
+- **The room asserts `checkLedger`** after every world tick in development and tests, together with its own invariant (no ship removed while the ledger counts its player in the match).

+- **Test-only settings** (never read by the production entry): `startGameServer({ matchTuning })` overrides the rules (for example a short seat reservation) and pins the source layout; the dev entry reads `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_SOURCES`.
- The slice uses Sun and Moon.

The purse beside the game shows your gold, your rubbings and what the last duel took or gave. A player who drops keeps their seat, ship and rubbings for 60 seconds (a fighter away from a duel for ten seconds forfeits it); one who never returns, or quits, leaves a recovery cache at a dock, a chest others see when in sight. Moor there and hold E to claim one rubbing of a type you lack.

The standalone duel (the combat spike, §18 stage 1) runs beside it: "Create duel" makes a 1v1 duel whose code the second browser enters under "Join duel", and "Practice" fights a server-side dummy (idle or guarding). Keys (§8): WASD or the arrows move (hold back to guard), J light, K heavy, U and I specials, Shift dash, J and K together throw. The HUD shows both health bars, stamina, the round clock, the connection line (round trip, input delay, corrections) and the result; "Show hitboxes" draws hurtboxes and active hitboxes.

The map is generated from an ASCII sketch of one quarter, `assets/source/maps/sliceSeaSketch.ts`: edit it, then run `npm run map:build -- --from-sketch` (details in `assets/source/maps/README.md`). lines: - **Absence** (§12, on the world tick). A drop anywhere disconnects the player in the ledger at once; the ship stays in the world, grapplable, for the 60 s seat reservation. A fighter away from an unfinished duel for 10 s, counted in world ticks, forfeits it (both on one frame: no winner, reported as cancelled) and respawns as any loser, keeping the seat. Back before the deadline, the same player continues (`reconnectPlayer`; a fighter gets a snapshot bundle). Colyseus' `allowReconnection` is only an outer bound (70 s) that keeps the socket's slot: at the ledger's deadline the room expires the reservation and releases that slot; any other leave (consented, or the outer bound first) is a quit.

- **Message routing.** A duel's `duel-frames` and `duel-probe` go to its two fighters only, with `client.send`; the room routes `duel-input`, `duel-probe` echoes and `duel-ready` from a session to that session's duel and drops them from anyone else. In the browser, `SeaDuelRouter` listens for the duel messages once per match and hands them to the duel client of the moment (a message that beats the lobby's patch waits for it); the same `DuelClient` runs a standalone duel over `duelRoomTransport`.

- **Visibility (§16).** The state's new maps are filtered per client like `ships`: `grapples` (telegraphs, keyed by attacker: in a view when its attacker is in sight, or when it is the viewer's own or aimed at the viewer; each attempt has a twin entry with `defenderId` blank, which a viewer who sees the attacker but not the target gets instead), `markers` (a duel's position and reservation tick under an opaque key, nothing naming its fighters: in a view within the sight radius), `caches` (a recovery cache's position and dock, no contents: within the sight radius), `status` (a player's own mode, protection, cooldown, respawn tick, gold, rubbings, holds and theft choice: only the player's), `duels` (a duel's lobby: only its two fighters'). A ship in a duel or waiting to respawn is in no one else's view; its own player keeps it until it waits to respawn. A fighter or a player waiting to respawn sees no other ship, telegraph, marker or cache. Integration tests check the decoded state and the raw frames of a watcher in sight and a stranger out of it.

-- **One game per page.** The match page's Phaser game holds the sea scene and the arena scene (`MatchGame`); a duel puts the sea to sleep and starts the arena with that duel's client, and its end wakes the sea (`data-scene` says which shows). The duel HUD moves beside the canvas meanwhile. The standalone duel page's game holds only the arena. The helm is read during a duel (so a J tapped in the arena is not kept) but the sea gets neutral input.

+- **One game per page.** The match page's Phaser game (canvas renderer, see Rendering) holds the sea scene and the arena scene (`MatchGame`); a duel puts the sea to sleep and starts the arena with that duel's client, and its end wakes the sea (`data-scene` says which shows). The duel HUD moves beside the canvas meanwhile. The standalone duel page's game holds only the arena. The helm is read during a duel (so a J tapped in the arena is not kept) but the sea gets neutral input.

- **One clock.** The room steps the simulation 60 times a second with Colyseus `setFixedTimestep`. World logic runs on frames divisible by 3 (20 Hz); the room then mirrors the plain state into its Schema and updates the views, and Colyseus patches clients at 20 Hz. Integration tests measure both rates, also with eight sailing ships in one cluster.

- **The server alone writes state.** At sea, clients send only `input` messages, `{seq, frame, buttons, moveX, moveY}`, validated with zod (the grapple is a button: the rules choose its target, never the client). `InputGate` drops, and counts, messages over the rate cap (60 per second of match time) or over 128 bytes, malformed ones (axes outside [-1, 1] are rejected, not clamped), ones whose sequence number is not higher than the last, and ones tagged more than 30 frames ahead. A held input lapses to neutral after 15 frames. An accepted world input applies from the server's next step whatever frame it names, since sea clients do not predict; a duel input applies to exactly the frame it names (`docs/duel.md`). Unknown message types are dropped. Colyseus's own limits sit above these: WebSocket frames over 4 KiB and more than 240 messages a second disconnect.

- **Joining.** Matches and duels share the admission code (`apps/server/src/admission.ts`). Colyseus serves `create`, `join`, `joinOrCreate` and `joinById` over HTTP and reserves a seat before any room check, so a private match is guarded in three layers. The static `onAuth` runs before any seat is reserved: it refuses a mismatched protocol version (426), a request with neither or both of `code` and `createToken` or a malformed token (400), an unknown code (404) and a full match (409). A `create` carries a one-time 128-bit `createToken`; the room is registered with `filterBy(['code', 'createToken'])` and `onCreate` replaces the listing's metadata with `{code, custom}`, so no listing holds a token and a token-carrying request can only create. The room's `onJoin` is the backstop, and the only check `joinById` meets after `onAuth`: one seat with the creator's token, then only seats with the match's code (404 for another code, 403 otherwise). Refusal messages stay under 100 bytes. A caller who knows a room id can still hold seats with `joinById` until each reservation expires (15 s).

-- **Rendering.** The client draws the ships the server sent 100 ms in the past, interpolating between patches; the HUD lists their latest decoded state. The camera follows the player's ship over a Phaser tile map at 24 px a tile (the 480 px sight circle fits the 800 × 560 view) that leaves open sea to the background colour, keeping a software renderer fast. The sea does not predict; the duel arena does (above), and uses Phaser's canvas renderer so a machine without a GPU keeps its main thread free for the 4 ms client tick.

The collect → fight → steal → recover loop now works in the match room, and all five checks pass in this worktree. The integration suite went from 201.65 s to **117.17 s**. Nothing is committed, as the task asked; the changes are uncommitted in the worktree.

**Checks run here**
| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run typecheck` | pass |
| `npm run test:unit` | 900 pass |
| `npm run test:integration` | 73 pass in 117.17 s (under 150 s); the netcode harness tests stay green |
| `npm run build` | pass, smoke test included |
| Playwright, all 8 scenarios | 8/8 pass, and `check-report` accepts all 8 |

**What was built**
- **Ledger in the room** (`apps/server/src/MatchRoom.ts`, new `objectives.ts`): one ledger per match, seeded from the room's private randomness, with two sources per island at its docks. Every source is unlocked until the ruins feature locks them.
- **Collecting**: holding E moors the ship and keeps collecting (6 s), island sources first, then cache rubbings. Letting go of E, casting off, being grappled or disconnecting resets it. Starting a collection or claim ends protection one tick later.
- **Theft**: the winner gets a 5 s choice through a new `choose-theft` message (protocol version 6). The default applies at the deadline, and players return to the sea only after the ledger settles.
- **Disconnects and quits**: the world tick drives every timer. A drop keeps the ship and seat for 60 s. A fighter away 10 s forfeits the duel but keeps the seat. At the deadline the remaining rubbings go to a cache at the respawn dock. Every other leave, including Colyseus' 70 s bound firing first, is a quit into a cache at the nearest dock by sea.
- **Invariant**: the room checks the ledger and "no ship without a ledger player" after every tick in development and tests (off in production). Every integration test asserts no violations.
- **Hidden information**: gold, rubbings and theft options go only to their owner. Island types and cache contents go only to players moored there. A grapple's `defenderId` is blank for watchers who can't see the target, proven on raw frames.
- **Web**: a panel beside the game shows gold, rubbings, the last duel's result and the theft choice (keys 1/2 or a click). The HUD shows the island's types, cache contents and a hold progress bar; caches are drawn as chests.

**Things to know**
- **Renderer switched.** The sea-duel measurement failed with `Phaser.AUTO`: the duel tick's 95th percentile was 135 ms in headless Chromium. So the match game now uses the canvas renderer (8.5 ms host, 8.9 ms guest), as the task allowed if the measurement failed. `docs/architecture.md` records both numbers.
- **One timing set per test file.** Colyseus has one matchmaker per process, so each integration file gets one set of test-only timings. That's why the rubbing tests are split across three files.
- **How the budget was met.** Test-only overrides alone brought it to 263.64 s serially (the new tests added about 70 s). Running files in 3 parallel workers, with the harness files in a serial second group, brought it to 117.17 s. The harness group alone takes about 64 s, so the margin depends on the verifier's machine not being overloaded.
- **Wording not updated.** `policy.json`'s theft-loop description still says "held attack keys". I couldn't change it (not an owned path); the test taps keys and its title says so.
- **Not covered by any test:** clicking a theft button (only the key is tested), reconnecting after a duel forfeit but before the 60 s deadline, and the server-side theft-choice rate cap.

The completion file is written to `…/rubbings-theft-001/game.completion.json`, and the docs and README are updated.
